title: Current India–Pakistan contribution
text:
# India and Pakistan: what spending scenarios can establish

**AI-assisted contribution draft, 22 October 2026. Human verification pending. Proposed for the unified report, subject to team agreement.**

India and Pakistan expose a basic difficulty in forecasting alternative-protein demand: the available numbers often describe something other than purchases. National food accounts measure supply, surveys ask about willingness, and company directories record activity. Each helps frame a question, but none supplies a national series of repeated purchases of meat, dairy or egg alternatives. This section therefore asks how spending might evolve under explicit assumptions, and which observations would make those assumptions more credible. It does not estimate animal-food displacement or returns on funding.

The starting point is GFI India and Deloitte's published estimate of India's 2022 smart-protein market: INR 351 crore across plant-based meat, dairy and eggs. Its forward domestic scenarios also include fermentation-derived meat. This is an external model estimate, not audited retail turnover. The source does not clearly state its price base or retail valuation. Our calculation assumes nominal 2022 rupees and treats the estimate as a retail-spending anchor; inflating it and converting at the 2025 exchange rate gives about $45.3 million. The retained evidence provides no equivalent Pakistan national sales anchor. That missing baseline must not be described as zero sales.[^market]

The proxy model carries India's estimated spending per person forward with real income, urbanisation and an additional growth term. It transfers that path to Pakistan using relative income, urban share, animal-protein supply and industry-activity proxies. The relationships and parameter distributions are analyst choices, not coefficients fitted to alternative-protein purchases. The table reports the tenth, fiftieth and ninetieth percentiles across 10,000 assumption draws. These are conditional scenarios with untested calibration, in millions of US dollars at constant 2025 prices.[^model]

| Country | Year | Lower | Middle | Upper |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| India | 2026 | 69 | 93 | 125 |
| India | 2030 | 102 | 188 | 334 |
| India | 2035 | 166 | 448 | 1,142 |
| Pakistan | 2026 | 1.5 | 3.6 | 6.6 |
| Pakistan | 2030 | 2.3 | 6.0 | 13.7 |
| Pakistan | 2035 | 3.6 | 11.8 | 36.1 |

The 2035 middle values correspond to roughly $0.28 per person in India and $0.040 in Pakistan. India's value is 1.22% of US plant-based retail spending per person observed in 2025; Pakistan's is about 0.17%. These are comparisons with a fixed historical benchmark, not shares of the US total market or comparisons with a 2035 US forecast. The US GFI/SPINS series covers broader categories, including prepared meals, so the ratio is illustrative rather than a matched product comparison.[^benchmark]

The results are sensitive to how the proxies are interpreted. The model's upper additional-growth assumption comes from growth in Indian job advertisements. Hiring activity may already reflect income growth; counting both could exaggerate expansion. A retained sensitivity that reduces this upper assumption lowers India's 2035 middle value from $448 million to $215 million. For Pakistan, removing the relative urban-share and animal-protein multipliers gives a middle value of $8.3 million and a tenth-to-ninetieth-percentile range of $2.6–25.3 million. Neither sensitivity is established as the correct specification. Together they show why the precision of the output exceeds the strength of the underlying relationships.[^sensitivity]

Consumer research does not close that gap. Bryant and colleagues' online study found high stated willingness to buy plant-based meat in India, but its Indian sample skewed urban, affluent and educated. It measured hypothetical intentions, not subsequent purchases. The retained bilateral literature uses different samples and questions; it cannot support a national India–Pakistan ranking of willingness or conversion. Four outcomes need separate measurement: stated willingness, first purchase, repeat purchase after incentives end, and a measured reduction in animal-food purchases. A larger spending total alone cannot tell us which occurred.[^behaviour]

Policy and technical progress can change the conditions for those purchases, but their effects require separate evidence. India's 2024 BioE3 announcement includes smart proteins and proposed biomanufacturing and Bio-AI infrastructure. This establishes policy intent, not the delivery of a particular product or its consumer uptake. Pakistan has halal institutions; their existence does not establish food authorization for a particular novel product. Product-specific regulatory and religious questions therefore remain distinct. The present scenarios exclude cultivated meat; a future approval would require a newly specified scenario rather than an undocumented addition to this one.[^policy]

AI should be treated as a mechanism to investigate, not an automatic market-growth bonus. The retained research discusses laboratory optimisation and protein design, while company and policy material describe possible applications. These sources do not establish a country-level AI effect on alternative-protein spending. Improvements in conventional dairy or poultry could also change relative competitiveness. A useful test would compare validated output, production cost and retail prices against a credible non-AI baseline, while checking whether any effect is already counted in the model's other growth assumptions.[^ai]

The same discipline should guide talent recommendations. GFI India's talent study draws on 20 industry responses and 19 academic leaders or administrators; it offers specific leads, not a national workforce census. Job advertisements likewise do not measure successful hiring or skill shortages. A bounded next step is to test an employer-nominated technical constraint in India and assess the feasibility of an ingredient-application pilot in Pakistan, with facilities, staff and baseline performance checked first. These are proposals for learning, not a ranking of expected returns. Comparable sales and repeated-purchase evidence would do more to strengthen the demand argument than another layer of proxy complexity.[^talent]

[^market]: GFI India and Deloitte, *Smart Protein Economic Analysis*, 2022-context analysis, methodology and final-page domestic-market table, [original report](https://gfi-india.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/GFI-India-economic-analysis.pdf). Precise publication date and price base are unstated; the upload path is not a publication date. Source mapping: C01–C03 in [claim map](../provenance/claims.md).
[^model]: Retained `altprotein_proxy_inputs.csv`, `altprotein_proxy_scenarios.csv` and `build_altprotein_proxy.py`; exact equations and assumptions in [proxy methods](../methods/proxy.md). IMF WEO October 2026 and World Bank WDI provide macro inputs. Mapping: C04–C06.
[^benchmark]: [GFI US retail market data](https://gfi.org/marketresearch/), 2025 sales; IMF population; retained comparison rows. The US anchor is $7.9 billion, or $23.106847 per person. Mapping: C07–C08.
[^sensitivity]: Retained 2035 sensitivity rows `market_value_drift_overlap_adjusted` and `market_value_without_urban_animal`; see methods for the exact changes. Mapping: C09–C10.
[^behaviour]: Christopher Bryant et al., “A Survey of Consumer Perceptions of Plant-Based and Clean Meat in the USA, India, and China,” *Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems* 3 (2019), [doi:10.3389/fsufs.2019.00011](https://doi.org/10.3389/fsufs.2019.00011); retained bilateral review and measurement audit. Mapping: C11–C12. The selective nine-study extraction package is not presented as a systematic national review.
[^policy]: Government of India, [BioE3 Cabinet approval, 24 August 2024](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2048568&lang=2&reg=3); Pakistan, [*Pakistan Halal Authority Act, 2016*](https://pakistancode.gov.pk/pdffiles/administrator1d376dbb967abb1d9ed2dcb3ae978dbc.pdf), especially establishment and functions. These are dated institutional sources, not a legal determination for a particular product. Mapping: C13–C14.
[^ai]: Dated source review in the retained AI-mechanism review, including Cosenza et al., [doi:10.1002/elsc.202300005](https://doi.org/10.1002/elsc.202300005), and Watson et al., [doi:10.1038/s41586-023-06415-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06415-8). The former's primary full text was not freshly recovered for this drafting pass. Mapping: C15.
[^talent]: Amrutha Girivasan and Chandana Tekkatte, GFI India, [*A comprehensive analysis of India's talent landscape for the smart protein sector*](https://gfi-india.org/resource/smart-protein-skills-mapping/), physical PDF page 10. The official website listing is dated 19 December 2025; the PDF itself is undated. Retained AltProtein.Jobs extracts and the author's capacity proposals are mapped in C16–C17. Pakistan's proposed pilot is a recommendation, not an observed programme.
note: Exact checked review-package document. Public dashboard release is author-authorized; human factual/code and scholarly review remain pending.
